newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court sets new trial in euthanasia case.
newsitem.headline: Canada court sets new trial in euthanasia case.

text.p: Canada's Supreme Court ordered a new trial on Thursday for farmer Robert Latimer, who was convicted of murdering his handicapped daughter, but denied him the full acquittal he sought.

The high-profile case was decided on legal technicalities such as whether his confession was admissible, rather than the issue of whether euthanasia was acceptable, but was nonetheless widely watched across Canada.

Latimer confessed to police that he placed his 12-year-old daughter Tracy in his pickup truck in 1993 and ran a hose from the exhaust pipe to the cab, causing her death from carbon monoxide. He initially said she had died in her sleep.

Tracy, a quadriplegiac with extreme cerebral palsy, was unable to walk, talk or feed herself and was in constant pain -- although Feika said she was in a school programme, loved music, rode a bus and interacted with people.
Latimer, who has been free on bail, sought to have his confession ruled inadmissible on the grounds he had not been properly informed of his rights and had not been informed he was under arrest.
But in a major blow the court ruled his rights had not been violated. It said however he should have a new trial, because even the prosecution agreed there had been jury tampering.
A year after his 1994 conviction for second-degree murder, it was learned police questioned potential jurors about their views on euthanasia, abortion and religion.
"The interference contravened a fundamental tenet of the criminal justice system," ruled Chief Justice Antonio Lamer in the 9-0 decision.
The man in charge of Saskatechewan's public prosecution office, Richard Quinney, said Latimer would be booked for second degree murder in his new trial.
He originally faced charges of first degree, premeditated murder but the jurors acquitted him of that. Consequently the prosecution would not press that charge again.
He said the retrial was likely to be sometime this year.
Canadians with disabilities in the lobby of the Supreme Court said they welcomed the fact that Latimer did not go free but urged the prosecution to press for first degree murder.

"This is not a mercy-killing. There is no mercy in killing someone who wants to live, and Tracy never had the opportunity to say yea or nay," said Irene Feika, leaning on a cane, who said she has arthritis, diabetes, asthma and stomach problems.
"I live with pain 24 hours a day. It wakes me up, it goes to bed with me when I go to sleep. Does that mean my family should put me down?"

Ruth Von Fuchs, a member of the Right to Die Society of Canada, told Reuters by phone from Toronto she thought someone in Tracy's position might have been a good candidate for "permanent sedation," where she would be kept technically alive but unconscious.
"Of all the people involved, she was the least able and the least deserving of this suffering," Von Fuchs said.
The Council of Canadians with Disabilities said it would be "criminal" not to charge Latimer with first degree murder.

"Tracy's disability cannot be allowed to become a mitigating factor in a judgment of Robert Latimer's actions to end her life, or the decision to prosecute Mr. Latimer for these actions," the council's Catherine Frazee said.

Latimer's lawyer, Mark Brayford, told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. that if his client were convicted and sentenced again for second-degree murder, they would probably try to have it declared "cruel and unusual punishment."
